newsitem.title: USA: More US steelmakers paying managers based on stock.
newsitem.headline: More US steelmakers paying managers based on stock.

text.p: U.S. steelmakers are increasingly linking executive pay to stock performance, signaling that an underperforming industry may be trying to reverse its reputation and be more shareholder friendly, industry officials and analysts say.
"This is an industry that has been underperforming to such an extent, it's mind boggling," said Chuck Bradford at UBS Securities.

Bradford said the industry has been underperforming largely because of weak pricing but then has been notorious for paying bonuses to senior executives from asset sale proceeds rather than recording proceeds as nonrecurring items.
"(Integrated steelmakers) need to tie management more to the shareholder," he said.

Shareholders of U.S. Steel Group, the nation's largest steelmaker, in '94 approved a compensation plan for senior officers that rewards them based on common stock performance, as well as factors including operating profit and shipments.
Shareholders of LTV Corp will vote this year on a
plan that for the first time will partially compensate top-level managers based on stock performance. A spokesman declined to elaborate, saying many details are preliminary.

But analysts familiar with the plan said managers, besides being partially compensated on stock performance, will be required to own a minimum of 10,600 shares each from a current average of about 1,000, and LTV's top five managers will be required to own 115,800 shares.

Another firm, Inland Steel Industries Inc, is implementing a plan approved by its board last month that partially rewards 150 managers on stock performance, said Bob Darnall, Inland's chairman, president and chief executive officer.

"The board has implemented performance-based stock incentives for about 150 key managers," Darnall said. The plan pays based on improvements in operating performance, dividend increases and stock price performance, he said.

Other large companies including Bethlehem Steel Corp and National Steel Corp do not tie compensation to stock price, but Bradford said all steelmakers should begin doing so to more closely align management and shareholder interests.

Integrated steel stocks have underperformed the market the past few years, failing to attract investors because the industry -- which downsized dramatically and bled red ink during the '80s -- is seen as stagnant, industry officials said.

Integrated steel stocks as a group fell 16 percent in '96 while the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 26 percent. The worst performer was Geneva Steel Co, which fell 56 percent, while the top performer was AK Steel Corp, which rose 15 percent.

AK Steel, by far the industry's most profitable company, does not tie compensation to stock performance but analysts said the company uses its strong cash flow to reward shareholders with things such as dividend increases and stock buybacks.
Shares of Inland Steel and LTV fell 20 percent and 13.5 percent last year, respectively.
Analysts said steelmakers' drive to reward executives on stock performance is necessary to convince investors they want to line shareholder pockets as well as their own.

"Share performance has been terrible...the companies announcing these compensation plans have to convince shareholders they're interested in share performance," said Aldo Mazzaferro at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
But boosting industry profits and shareholder wealth will demand that the industry consolidate further and reduce the number of players, Bradford said.
"The industry isn't making enough on its assets to keep it alive," he said. "I think they understand this but it hasn't sunk in yet what needs to be done."
He said there are too many steel companies supplying a few large customers, such as U.S. automakers, which leads to steelmakers cutting prices to win business.
There are at least half a dozen steelmakers who are considered major suppliers to large customers including auto and appliance makers.
"There should be three big steel companies," he said. "But how do you do that, I don't know. The problem has always been the government not allowing these big companies to merge."
